summary:
The Faroe Islands are a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Denmark's criminal law and document rules extend to the territory, while equality and family law are made locally beneath the Danish human-rights framework.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was legalised across the Kingdom of Denmark. The age of consent was then set at 18 for male same-sex relations, and the territory did not follow Denmark's 1977 move to a gender-neutral age of 15 until 1988.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation became a criminal offence only on 1 January 2007, when the anti-discrimination law took effect. Anyone who publicly makes a statement that threatens, insults or degrades a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or to imprisonment for up to two years. This made the Faroe Islands the last Northern European country to ban discrimination and harassment based on sexual orientation.

Before that law existed, violence against gay people went legally unaddressed. In 2006 the openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls. Police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law prohibited discrimination against sexual minorities. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression aggravated by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012.

In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men who intended to assault them in Tórshavn; the group had not been attacked anywhere else on its tour. The first gay pride march that year provoked substantial controversy.

Religiously motivated opposition sits openly in Faroese politics. On 7 September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister Johanna Sigurdardottir and her partner, citing his religion. In July 2015 he demanded that Pride be banned; singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him, and his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality. He has also compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and urged that the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the town centre.

Expression around LGBT life has been a recurring flashpoint. In June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter to the editor, 'Hvar eru vit á veg?', attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar, condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture' and asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'.

Petitioning has been extensive relative to a population of about 47,000. An internet petition after the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen collected 20,000 signatures, reported in the same period as demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics, which the territory then lacked; eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 signatures by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. A petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures.

Same-sex marriage was adopted in 2017, later than in the rest of the Nordic region and after friction between church and state.
tangentialFactors:
The Faroe Islands were the last Northern European country to legislate against discrimination based on sexual orientation, doing so only in 2007, and same-sex marriage followed a decade later in 2017 — both later than the territory's Nordic neighbours.

Public hostility has been expressed through institutional channels as well as on the street: a parliamentary speaker's published letter, a party leader's repeated demands to displace or ban Pride, and a state-banquet boycott all date from 2010 to 2015, alongside organised counter-signature campaigns such as the 1,262-name petition against same-sex marriage.

Signature volumes are unusually large relative to the resident population of about 47,000, indicating sustained public mobilisation on both sides of the question.

The 2006 Rasmussen case shows that where no anti-discrimination provision existed, police declined to investigate a violent assault on a gay man; the pattern of street violence documented in 2005 and 2006 is not matched in the sources by any conviction or penalty.
localsOnly:
Residents are covered by the anti-discrimination law in force since 1 January 2007, which makes public threats, insults or degrading statements against a group on grounds including sexual orientation punishable by a fine or by up to two years' imprisonment.

Equality and family law, including the 2017 same-sex marriage statute, are made by the Løgting in Tórshavn rather than by the Danish parliament, so residence-related rights in these areas follow Faroese legislation.

Local employers, service providers and public bodies fall within the 2007 prohibition, which took effect later than equivalent rules in neighbouring Nordic jurisdictions.
outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced material in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, the procedure or criteria for changing sex markers on identity documents, or which Danish document rules apply unchanged in the Faroe Islands. This is unresolved rather than established as absent.

Entry and visa requirements for visitors, including any screening that could disclose a traveller's trans status, are not covered by the available sources; the extent to which Danish and Realm entry rules apply here verbatim is not sourced.

The inventory contains nothing on access to gender-affirming healthcare, on facilities such as toilets and changing rooms, or on whether hate-crime sentencing enhancements exist beyond the base anti-discrimination penalty.

Conviction and sentencing data for offences under the 2007 provision are not available in the sources, so its enforcement record cannot be assessed.
